questions.question_text: A dataset has a mean of $\mu = 45$ and a standard deviation of $\sigma = 4$. What is the $z$-score of the value $x = 39$?

options.why: Calculated $\mu - x$ instead of $x - \mu$, which reverses the sign of the z-score.
Found the difference $39 - 45$ but did not divide by the standard deviation.
Inverted the fraction, dividing the standard deviation by the difference instead of the other way round.

questions.question_text: A dataset has a mean of $\mu = 7.4$ and a standard deviation of $\sigma = 1.5$. What is the $z$-score of the value $x = 8.6$?

options.why: Calculated $\mu - x$ instead of $x - \mu$, so the value appears to be below the mean.
Found the difference $8.6 - 7.4$ but did not divide by the standard deviation.
Inverted the fraction, dividing the standard deviation by the difference.

questions.question_text: The masses of loaves of bread from a bakery have a mean of $640$ g and a standard deviation of $25$ g. What is the $z$-score of a loaf with a mass of $690$ g?

options.why: Calculated $\mu - x$ instead of $x - \mu$, giving a negative score for a loaf that is above the mean.
Stopped at the difference $690 - 640$ without dividing by the standard deviation.
Inverted the fraction, dividing the standard deviation by the difference.

questions.question_text: Journey times on a train line have a mean of $46$ minutes and a standard deviation of $9$ minutes. What is the $z$-score of a journey of $32$ minutes, correct to two decimal places?

options.why: Calculated $\mu - x$ instead of $x - \mu$, reversing the sign of a journey that is below the mean.
Cut the decimal off after two places instead of rounding $-1.5555...$, which rounds to $-1.56$.
Stopped at the difference $32 - 46$ without dividing by the standard deviation.

questions.question_text:
In a test the mean was $72$ and the standard deviation was $6$.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{Student} & \text{Ava} & \text{Ben} & \text{Cara} & \text{Dan} \\ \hline \text{Mark} & 78 & 69 & 72 & 66 \end{array}$
Which student has a $z$-score of $-0.5$?

options.why: Ignores the negative sign; Ava is above the mean, so her z-score is $+1$.
Cara's mark equals the mean, so her z-score is $0$, not $-0.5$.
Dan is $6$ below the mean, a full standard deviation, so his z-score is $-1$.

questions.question_text: A value in a dataset has a $z$-score of $-2.4$. Which statement describes this value?

options.text: It is $2.4$ standard deviations below the mean.
It is $2.4$ units below the mean.
options.why: Reads the z-score as a raw difference; it counts standard deviations, not units of the original measurement.

options.text: It is $2.4$ standard deviations above the mean.
options.why: Ignores the negative sign, which is what places the value below the mean.
Treats the z-score as a multiplier of the mean rather than a count of standard deviations from it.

questions.solution_text:
The size of a $z$-score is the number of standard deviations from the mean, and a negative $z$-score means below the mean.
The value is $2.4$ standard deviations below the mean.

questions.question_text: Sam's mark in a test gives him a $z$-score of $0$. What does this tell you about his mark?

options.text: His mark is equal to the mean of the test.

options.why: Confuses the standardised score with the raw mark; the raw mark is only zero if the mean is zero.

options.text: His mark is one standard deviation above the mean.
options.why: Reads $z = 0$ as 'no deviations counted yet' and then adds one; a z-score of $1$ is one standard deviation above.

options.text: His mark was the lowest in the test.
options.why: Treats $0$ as the smallest possible z-score, but z-scores below the mean are negative.

questions.solution_text:
$z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$
The fraction is zero only when its numerator is zero, so $x - \mu = 0$.
Sam's mark is equal to the mean of the test.

questions.question_text:
The number of goals scored by a team in each of eight matches was
$4, \ 7, \ 5, \ 9, \ 6, \ 5, \ 8, \ 4$
What is the $z$-score of the highest score, correct to two decimal places? Use the population standard deviation.

options.why: Used the sample standard deviation $s_x = 1.8516...$ instead of the population standard deviation $\sigma = 1.7320...$
Divided by the variance $3$ rather than by the standard deviation $\sqrt{3}$.
Calculated $\mu - x$ instead of $x - \mu$, giving a negative score for the highest value.

questions.solution_text:
From the statistics mode of the calculator,
$\mu = 6$
$\sigma = 1.7320...$
The highest score is $x = 9$.
$z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$
$= \dfrac{9 - 6}{1.7320...}$
$= 1.7320...$
$\approx 1.73$
